L2200@P104-105: Section 3 - The Nature of Infinity106
L2201@P105:  We start this section by discussing a couple of examples which indicate some of the
L2202@P105: counterintuitive properties of infinite sets.
L2203@P105: Hilbert's Hotel: Where They Never Say, "Sorry, We're Full Up"
L2204@P105:  In an ordinary hotel (one with 20, 200, or 2000 rooms), once every room is full, a late-arriving
L2205@P105: guest cannot obtain an unoccupied room. David Hilbert, one of the greatest mathematicians of the
L2206@P105: early twentieth century, concocted the following example, which is called Hilbert's Hotel in his
L2207@P105: honor.
L2208@P105:  Imagine a hotel with an infinite number of rooms, one room for every positive whole number.
L2209@P105: Suppose that every room is occupied, and a guest arrives looking for an empty room. Rather than
L2210@P105: turn the guest (and the accompanying cash) out in the cold, the hotel manager simply moves the
L2211@P105: occupant of Room 1 to Room 2, the occupant of Room 2 to Room 3, the occupant of Room 3 to
L2212@P105: Room 4, etc. After all this moving is done, every former occupant still has a room, but Room 1 is
L2213@P105: now free, and the new guest moves in!
L2214@P105:  Later in the evening, the hotel is still full, and an infinite number of new guests arrive. Not to
L2215@P105: worry. The manager gives each new guest a number, just as one would at a store where you have to
L2216@P105: wait in line. While the guests are in the bar, the manager moves the occupant of Room 1 to Room
L2217@P105: 2, the occupant of Room 2 to Room 4, the occupant of Room 3 to Room 6, etc. All the previous
L2218@P105: occupants are now in even-numbered rooms. The odd-numbered rooms are now vacant, so new
L2219@P105: Guest 1 moves into Room 1, new Guest 2 moves into Room 3, new Guest 3 moves into Room 5,
L2220@P105: and so on. Everyone is happy (especially the stockholders)!
